learning_objectives.description: Apply port mapping between host and containers
Convert between bytes and strings in Python
Create and configure basic TCP sockets

questions.stem: With the course mapping 127.0.0.1:9050:9000, which host port serves the Portainer HTTP interface?

feedback.correct: Correct: 9050 is the published host port in the course configuration.
feedback.incorrect: Review the Portainer setup section in Prerequisites.md

questions.explanation: The course publishes host TCP 9050 to the container HTTP listener on 9000. HTTPS 9443 is a different endpoint and is not implied by this mapping.

questions.stem: Which command starts the Docker service in WSL2 (without systemd)?

options.text: docker start
systemctl start docker
sudo service docker start
wsl --start docker

feedback.correct: Correct! The service command works in WSL2 without systemd.
feedback.incorrect: In WSL2 without systemd, use 'sudo service docker start'.

questions.explanation: In WSL2 without systemd enabled, services are managed with 'sudo service <name> start'.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between a Docker image and a container?

options.text: They are the same thing with different names
An image is a running instance of a container
A container is an instance created from an image and may be running or stopped
Images are created by stopping containers

feedback.correct: Exactly! Think of images as templates and containers as instances.

questions.explanation: An image is a read-only template (like a mould); a container is a runnable instance created from that image.

questions.stem: In the command 'docker run -p 8080:80 nginx', what does 8080 represent?

options.text: The container's internal port
The host machine's port
The maximum number of connections
The nginx version number

feedback.incorrect: Remember: -p HOST:CONTAINER. The first number is always the host port.

questions.explanation: The format is -p HOST:CONTAINER. Here, 8080 is the host port that maps to container port 80.

questions.stem: Assume curl is installed in a normal bridge-network Alpine container and nothing listens on its port 9050. Why does 'curl localhost:9050' fail although Portainer is published on the host at 9050?

options.text: Alpine containers don't support the curl command
Portainer blocks access from other containers
localhost inside a container refers to that container, not the host
Port 9050 is reserved for system processes

feedback.correct: Exactly! Each container has its own localhost.

questions.explanation: A normal bridge-network container has its own loopback. Host access depends on Docker Desktop/native Engine routing and the service bind address; a host loopback-only listener is not automatically reachable via a bridge gateway.

questions.stem: To convert the string 'Hello' to bytes in Python, use: 'Hello'.___('utf-8')
questions.hint: This method is the opposite of decode()

feedback.correct: Correct! encode() converts strings to bytes for network transmission.
feedback.incorrect: Remember: ENcode puts data ON the wire (str → bytes).

questions.explanation: encode() converts str to bytes; decode() converts bytes to str. This is essential for network programming.

questions.stem: To safely decode bytes that might contain invalid UTF-8 characters, use: data.decode('utf-8', errors='___')

feedback.correct: Well done! Using error handling prevents crashes on invalid data.
feedback.incorrect: Without error handling, invalid UTF-8 raises UnicodeDecodeError.

questions.explanation: Using errors='replace' substitutes invalid bytes with the Unicode replacement character (U+FFFD), preventing exceptions.

questions.stem: On the Linux teaching server, which option is set before bind() to permit address reuse under the OS rules after a previous connection, without allowing takeover of an active conflicting listener? sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.___, 1)
questions.hint: This socket option allows reusing the address

feedback.correct: Correct: SO_REUSEADDR is useful for this Linux development-server pattern.
feedback.incorrect: The option is SO_REUSEADDR; its effect is subject to the operating system’s address-reuse rules.

questions.explanation: SO_REUSEADDR changes the OS address-reuse checks and can help a server restart after prior TCP connections. It does not bypass an active conflicting listener; behaviour is platform-dependent.

questions.stem: Which struct format string correctly packs a port number (2 bytes) in network byte order (big-endian)?

options.text: struct.pack('H', port)
struct.pack('!H', port)
struct.pack('h', port)
struct.pack('I', port)

feedback.correct: Correct: !H gives this protocol an explicitly big-endian unsigned 16-bit field. Other protocols may specify a different byte order.
feedback.incorrect: The '!' prefix is essential for network byte order. 'H' = unsigned short.

questions.explanation: The '!' prefix specifies network byte order (big-endian). 'H' is an unsigned short (2 bytes). Without '!', native byte order is used, which may be wrong.

questions.stem: Assume mycontainer was created without --rm and uses a normal writable layer (no tmpfs). After 'docker stop mycontainer' completes, what happens to its container object and writable-layer data?

options.text: The container and all its data are permanently deleted
The container enters 'Exited' state; data is preserved
Data is automatically backed up to a volume
The container is removed but volumes are kept

feedback.correct: Correct! stop preserves the container; rm removes it.

questions.explanation: docker stop gracefully stops a container but preserves it and its data. Use 'docker rm' to remove a stopped container.
